summary: Specifies how to use the US National Security Agency's Commercial National Security Algorithm (CNSA) Suite with S/MIME, as defined in RFC 8551. It applies to US national security systems and others who choose to follow that algorithm policy.

eli5.summary: The government has a short list of approved secret codes. This tells email programs which of those codes to use for protected email.

subtitle: Using NSA-approved cryptographic algorithms in secure email.

tldr.problem: US National Security Systems and government agencies need consistent cryptographic algorithm policies that provide strong security while remaining practical in the near term before the transition to quantum-resistant cryptography.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8755 specifies how to use the NSA's Commercial National Security Algorithm (CNSA) Suite—a curated set of commercial cryptographic algorithms—with S/MIME, the secure email standard, defining precise requirements for signing, key establishment, and encryption.
tldr.outcome: Implementations can achieve CNSA compliance by following the specified algorithm profiles: using SHA-384 for hashing, ECDSA or RSA for signatures, ECDH or RSA for key establishment, and AES-GCM (preferred) or AES-CBC for content encryption.

today: RFC 8755 remains the definitive profile for using CNSA Suite algorithms in S/MIME within US National Security Systems and other high-value government systems. As organizations transition toward post-quantum cryptography in the coming years, this RFC serves as a bridge: it provides proven, standardized algorithms that are strong against current quantum computers while remaining practical to deploy, allowing systems to avoid the costly disruption of two major cryptographic transitions in quick succession.

sections.title: Purpose and Applicability
sections.content:
The National Security Agency (NSA) publishes the Commercial National Security Algorithm (CNSA) Suite to define cryptographic algorithm policies for national security applications. Rather than defining new algorithms, the CNSA Suite curates existing, widely available commercial algorithms that have proven secure and interoperable. RFC 8755 specifies how to use CNSA Suite algorithms in S/MIME (Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions), the standard for secure email defined in RFC 8551.

The document applies directly to all US National Security Systems that use S/MIME messaging, as described in NIST Special Publication 800-59. It is also appropriate for other US Government systems processing high-value information and is made publicly available for any organization that chooses to adopt the same cryptographic policies. The CNSA Suite was established to provide "near-term flexibility" in meeting security requirements while anticipating a future transition to quantum-resistant cryptography—the suite allows vendors and customers to avoid making two major transitions in a short timeframe.
sections.eli5: The NSA published a list of the safest secret codes that computers can use. This document explains how to use that list when sending protected emails.

sections.title: The CNSA Suite Algorithms
sections.content:
The CNSA Suite specifies a small set of algorithms that S/MIME implementations must use to achieve compliance. SHA-384 is the sole message digest (hashing) algorithm, selected for its strength and availability. For digital signatures, implementations must support ECDSA (Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm) using the P-384 elliptic curve or RSA signatures with modulus sizes of either 3,072 or 4,096 bits. RSA signatures must use either RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 (the traditional approach) or RSASSA-PSS (the preferred scheme for new applications), both paired with SHA-384.

For key establishment—the process of creating shared secrets between sender and recipient—the suite offers ECDH (Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman) with the P-384 curve or RSA key transport with either RSAES-PKCS1-v1_5 or RSAES-OAEP. For content encryption, AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) with a 256-bit key must be used in either GCM (Galois Counter Mode), which is preferred because it provides authenticated encryption, or CBC (Cipher Block Chaining) mode, acceptable for compatibility with existing systems. All S/MIME applications use these same algorithms in different combinations depending on the message type and key establishment method.
sections.eli5: The approved secret codes are: SHA-384 for mixing data (to check if it changed), two ways to sign things (one using elliptic curves, one using RSA), two ways to share secret keys, and two ways to scramble the message itself.

sections.title: Digital Signatures
sections.content:
RFC 8755 defines precise requirements for generating and validating digital signatures in S/MIME. ECDSA signatures using SHA-384 and the P-384 curve must encode the signature output (the r and s values) in a specific binary format called ECDSA-Sig-Value. When used, the algorithm identifier must omit parameters from its encoding. For RSA signatures, implementations must choose between RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 (the simpler but older method) and RSASSA-PSS (which includes random padding for additional security). If using PSS, very specific parameters are required: SHA-384 for hashing, MGF1-SHA384 for the mask generation function, a salt length of 48 octets, and a trailer field value of 1.

Public key certificates used to verify signatures must comply with the CNSA Suite certificate profile defined in RFC 8603. RSA key pairs must use exponents meeting specific constraints, and the signature algorithm identifiers are embedded in the CMS (Cryptographic Message Syntax) structures. Implementations must treat any signature that does not meet these requirements as invalid, ensuring strict compliance with the CNSA policy.
sections.eli5: When someone signs an email, they use either elliptic curves or RSA with SHA-384. The standards are very specific about exactly how to do this and what counts as a valid signature.

sections.title: Key Establishment and Content Encryption
sections.content:
When S/MIME sends encrypted email to recipients, it must establish a shared key known only to the sender and recipient. The CNSA Suite offers two main approaches. ECDH (Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman) is the preferred method: the sender generates an ephemeral (temporary) key pair, derives a shared secret using the recipient's static public key (obtained from an X.509 certificate), and then applies a key derivation function (KDF) based on SHA-384 to generate a key-encryption key. This intermediate key encrypts the content-encryption key using AES-256 Key Wrap with Padding. RSA key transport is an alternative: the sender simply encrypts the content-encryption key directly using the recipient's RSA public key, either with RSAES-PKCS1-v1_5 or RSAES-OAEP.

For content encryption, the message data itself is encrypted using AES-256. In AES-GCM mode (preferred), the encryption produces both ciphertext and an authentication tag that ensures both confidentiality and authenticity. The implementation must generate a fresh random nonce (initialization vector) for each message and never reuse the same nonce with the same key, as doing so breaks security catastrophically. In AES-CBC mode (acceptable for compatibility), the encryption requires a random 16-octet initialization vector. AES-GCM is recommended because it provides authenticated encryption in a single operation, while CBC requires separate authentication mechanisms.
sections.eli5: To encrypt an email, you create a temporary key with the recipient using their public key, convert that into an encryption key, scramble the message with AES-256, and include an authentication code to prove nothing was changed. GCM does all this in one go; CBC is an older way that needs extra steps.

sections.title: Implementation and Security Requirements
sections.content:
RFC 8755 includes several important security requirements. Implementations must use secure random number generation when creating initialization vectors, ephemeral keys, and other cryptographic values; RFC 4086 provides guidance on this. The nonce handling in AES-GCM is particularly critical: each message requires a freshly generated nonce, and reusing a nonce with the same key completely compromises confidentiality. Implementations must carefully manage trust anchors (root certificates) that validate the sender's and recipient's certificates, and these roots must be securely provisioned before use.

The document notes that authenticated encryption modes like AES-GCM with AES-authenticated-enveloped-data are preferable to AES-CBC with unauthenticated enveloped-data, as they provide stronger security guarantees. The certificate profile referenced (RFC 8603) ensures that public key certificates used with CNSA algorithms meet the necessary security properties. Because the CNSA Suite algorithms themselves are well-established from prior RFCs and standards, the security considerations sections in those referenced documents (such as RFC 5652 for CMS, RFC 5753 for ECC algorithms, and RFC 3565 for AES) apply here as well.
sections.eli5: The rules are strict about how to pick random numbers, never reusing scrambling codes, and trusting the right certificates. Using the fancy new scrambling mode (GCM) is safer than the older way (CBC).
